title: The Engineer’s Thumb
paragraphs: Of all the puzzles brought to my friend Sherlock Holmes during our long friendship, only two reached him through me: the affair of Mr. Hatherley’s thumb and that of Colonel Warburton’s madness. The latter perhaps gave greater scope to an acute and original observer. But the former began so strangely and contained such dramatic incidents that it may better deserve a written account, even though it offered fewer opportunities for the deductive reasoning by which Holmes obtained his remarkable results. I believe the newspapers have told the story more than once. Yet, as with all such accounts, its effect is diminished when presented _en bloc_ in half a column of print. It is far more striking when the facts unfold before one’s eyes and each fresh discovery clears another part of the mystery, leading step by step towards the whole truth. The circumstances impressed me deeply at the time. Two years have passed, but that impression has scarcely faded.

The events I am about to recount happened in the summer of 1889, shortly after my marriage. I had returned to civilian medical practice and finally left Holmes alone in his Baker Street rooms. Nevertheless, I visited him frequently and occasionally persuaded him to abandon his Bohemian habits enough to call on us. My practice grew steadily. Living fairly near Paddington Station, I acquired several patients among the railway staff. One, whom I had cured of a painful and persistent illness, never tired of praising my abilities. He tried to send me every sick person over whom he had any influence.

One morning, just before seven, the maid knocked to wake me. Two men from Paddington were waiting in my consulting-room. Experience had taught me that railway cases were rarely minor, so I dressed quickly and hurried downstairs. As I approached, my old ally, the guard, came out and carefully closed the door behind him.
“I’ve brought him,” he whispered, jerking his thumb back over his shoulder. “He’s safely inside.”
“What have you brought?” I asked. His manner suggested he had shut some curious creature in my room.

“A new patient,” he whispered. “Thought I’d bring him myself, so he couldn’t get away. There he is, safe and sound. Must be off now, Doctor. I have my duties, just like you.” And my faithful recruiter departed before I could even thank him.

In the consulting-room I found a gentleman sitting beside the table. He wore a modest suit of heather tweed and had placed a soft cloth cap on my books. Around one of his hands he had wrapped a handkerchief, its surface blotched with blood. He was young—no more than twenty-five, I thought—with a strong, masculine face. But he was extremely pale and seemed deeply agitated, as though controlling his emotions required all his strength of mind.

“I am sorry to wake you so early, Doctor,” he said. “I had a very serious accident during the night. I arrived by train this morning and asked at Paddington where I could find a doctor. A kindly fellow brought me here himself. I gave your maid my card, but I see she left it on the side-table.”

I picked up the card and read it: ‘Mr. Victor Hatherley, hydraulic engineer, 16A Victoria Street, third floor.’ Such were my visitor’s name, profession, and address. “I am sorry to have kept you waiting,” I said, sitting in my library chair. “You have just completed a night journey, I gather, which is a monotonous business in itself.”

“Oh, I could hardly call the night I have just spent monotonous,” he replied, laughing. He leaned back and shook with loud, ringing laughter. Every medical instinct I possessed protested against the sound.
“Stop!” I cried. “Compose yourself!” I poured out some water from a carafe.

It did no good. He had surrendered to one of those hysterical fits that sometimes overcome strong people after a great crisis has passed. Eventually he recovered himself, looking exhausted and very pale.
“I have behaved like a fool,” he gasped.
“Not at all. Drink this.” I added a splash of brandy to the water. Colour began returning to his bloodless cheeks.
“That is better!” he said. “Now, Doctor, would you kindly look at my thumb—or rather, at the place where it used to be?”

He unwound the handkerchief and extended his hand. Even my experienced nerves recoiled at the sight. Four fingers projected above a dreadful red, spongy surface where the thumb should have been. It had been cut or torn away at its base.
“Good heavens!” I exclaimed. “A terrible wound. You must have lost a great deal of blood.”

“Yes. I fainted when it happened and must have remained unconscious for a long time. When I woke, it was still bleeding. I bound one end of my handkerchief tightly around the wrist and used a twig to tighten it.”
“Excellent! You ought to have become a surgeon.”
“It was a hydraulic problem, you see, so it fell within my own field.”
“A very heavy, sharp implement caused this,” I said, examining the wound.
“Something like a cleaver,” he replied.
“An accident, I assume?”
“Certainly not an accident.”
“What! Someone tried to murder you?”
“Most decidedly murderous.”
“That is horrifying.”
I sponged and cleaned the wound, dressed it, then covered it with cotton padding and carbolic bandages. He leaned back without flinching, though occasionally he bit his lip.
“How does that feel?” I asked when I had finished.
“Splendid! Your brandy and bandaging have made a new man of me. I was terribly weak, but then I have endured a great deal.”
“Perhaps you should not discuss it. It is clearly putting a strain on your nerves.”

“Oh, no, not now. I shall have to give my account to the police. Between ourselves, though, if I did not have this wound as convincing evidence, I would be surprised if they believed my statement. It is an extraordinary story, and I have very little proof to support it. Even if they believe me, the clues I can supply are so indefinite that it remains doubtful whether justice will be done.”
“Ah!” I exclaimed. “If there is anything in the nature of a mystery that you wish to see solved, I strongly advise you to consult my friend Sherlock Holmes before approaching the official police.”
“I have heard of him,” my visitor answered. “I would be delighted if he took an interest, though naturally I must also involve the police. Would you be kind enough to introduce me to him?”
“Better still, I shall take you there myself.”
“I would be very much obliged to you.”
“Let us take a cab together. We should arrive in time to share his breakfast. Do you feel strong enough?”
“Yes. I shall not rest until I have told someone.”

“Then my servant will call a cab. I shall join you in a moment.” I hurried upstairs to explain briefly to my wife. Five minutes later I was in a hansom beside my new acquaintance, on our way to Baker Street.

As I expected, Holmes was lounging in his sitting-room in a dressing-gown, reading the personal notices in _The Times_ and smoking his pre-breakfast pipe. Its contents were the tobacco plugs and half-smoked remnants left from the day before, carefully dried and collected at one corner of the mantelpiece. He welcomed us with quiet friendliness, ordered more bacon and eggs, and joined us for a hearty breakfast. Afterwards he settled our visitor on the sofa, put a pillow beneath his head, and left a glass of brandy and water within reach.

“Plainly your experience has been far from ordinary, Mr. Hatherley,” he said. “Lie back and make yourself entirely comfortable. Tell us whatever you can, but stop if you grow tired, and take a little stimulant to maintain your strength.”

“Thank you,” my patient replied. “But I have felt transformed since the doctor dressed my hand, and breakfast has completed the cure. To take as little of your valuable time as possible, I shall begin my strange account at once.”

Holmes settled into his large armchair, wearing the tired, heavy-lidded expression that concealed his keen, eager nature. I sat opposite him. Together we listened without interruption to our visitor’s remarkable story.

“First,” he began, “I am an orphan and unmarried, living alone in London lodgings. I work as a hydraulic engineer. During my seven-year apprenticeship with Venner & Matheson, the well-known Greenwich firm, I gained extensive experience. Two years ago, after completing my apprenticeship and inheriting a reasonable sum on my poor father’s death, I decided to establish my own business. I rented professional rooms in Victoria Street.

“Starting independently in business is probably discouraging for everyone. For me it has been exceptionally so. In two years I have had three consultations and one small commission: nothing else whatsoever. My total receipts amount to twenty-seven pounds ten shillings. Every day I sat in my little office from nine until four, waiting. Finally my spirits began to fail, and I came to believe I would never establish a practice at all.

“Yesterday, however, just as I was preparing to leave, my clerk announced a gentleman who wished to discuss business. He brought a card engraved ‘Colonel Lysander Stark’. The colonel followed close behind him. He was a little taller than the average man, but extraordinarily, almost unbelievably thin. I doubt I have ever seen a thinner man. His face narrowed into a sharp nose and chin, and the skin of his cheeks stretched tightly across projecting bones. Yet he seemed naturally lean rather than ill: his eyes were bright, his step brisk, and his manner confident. His clothes were plain but neat. I judged him nearer forty than thirty.
“‘Mr. Hatherley?’ he asked with a trace of a German accent. ‘You have been recommended to me as a man who combines professional skill with discretion and the ability to keep a secret.’
“I bowed, flattered as any young man would be by such words. ‘May I ask who spoke so highly of me?’
“‘Well, perhaps it would be better if I did not tell you that at this particular moment. The same person informed me that you are an orphan, unmarried, and living alone in London.’

“‘That is entirely correct,’ I replied. ‘But forgive me: I do not see how these facts concern my professional qualifications. I understood you wished to consult me about a matter connected with my profession?’

“‘Certainly. Everything I say is relevant, as you will discover. I have a commission for you, but absolute secrecy is essential—absolute secrecy, you understand. Naturally we can expect that more readily from a man living alone than from one surrounded by a family.’
“‘If I give my word to keep a secret,’ I said, ‘you can rely on it absolutely.’
“While I was speaking, he examined me very closely indeed. I thought I had never encountered eyes so suspicious and searching.
“‘Will you promise, then?’ he asked at last.
“‘Yes. I give you my word.’
“‘Complete silence beforehand, throughout, and afterwards? Not a single reference to the matter, either spoken or written?’
“‘I have already given you my promise.’
“‘Very good.’ Suddenly he jumped up, sped across the room, and flung the door wide. Nobody was in the passage.

“‘Excellent,’ he said on returning. ‘Clerks sometimes take an interest in their employers’ affairs. Now we can speak safely.’ He drew his chair very close to mine and again subjected me to that thoughtful, questioning stare.
“The gaunt man’s peculiar behaviour began to fill me with disgust and something close to fear. Even my anxiety about losing a client could not keep me from showing impatience.
“‘Please tell me the nature of your business, sir,’ I said. ‘My time is valuable.’ Heaven forgive that last remark, but the words escaped me.
“‘Would fifty guineas suit you for one night’s work?’ he asked.
“‘It would suit me admirably.’

“‘I say a night, though an hour would be more accurate. I merely want your assessment of a hydraulic stamping machine that has developed a fault. Show us what is wrong, and we can soon repair it ourselves. How does that commission sound?’
“‘The work seems slight, and the fee very generous.’
“‘Exactly. We need you to take the last train tonight.’
“‘To what destination?’
“‘Eyford in Berkshire. A small place near Oxfordshire’s border, within seven miles of Reading. There is a Paddington train that would get you there around a quarter past eleven.’
“‘Very well, then.’
“‘I shall meet you there with a carriage.’
“‘There will be a drive afterwards?’
“‘Yes. Our little property is well out in the country, a good seven miles from Eyford Station.’
“‘Then we will hardly arrive before midnight. Presumably there will be no train returning at that hour. I should have to stay overnight.’
“‘Yes, we can easily make up a bed for you.’
“‘That is inconvenient. Could I come at a more suitable time?’

“‘We have decided that a late visit would be best. To compensate you for any inconvenience, we offer a young and unknown man a fee large enough to obtain advice from the very leaders of your profession. Naturally, if you would prefer to withdraw from the business, there is still plenty of time to do so.’

“I thought of the fifty guineas and how very useful that money would be to me. ‘Not at all,’ I replied. ‘I shall gladly arrange things as you wish. I would merely like a clearer understanding of what you want me to do.’

“‘Of course. It is natural that the promise of secrecy we required should have stirred your curiosity. I have no wish to commit you to anything until you have heard the whole affair. Are you quite sure we are safe from anyone overhearing?’
“‘Completely certain.’
“‘Then here is the situation. You probably know that fuller’s-earth is valuable and occurs in only one or two places in England?’
“‘So I have heard.’

“‘A little while ago I bought a small property—a very small one—within ten miles of Reading. Fortunately, I discovered fuller’s-earth in one field. On investigation, however, my deposit proved relatively small: it connected two much larger deposits, one on either side, both on my neighbours’ land. These good people were entirely unaware that what lay beneath their fields was as valuable as a gold mine. Clearly it would benefit me to buy before they discovered their land’s real worth. Unfortunately, I had no capital with which to make such a purchase. I told a few friends in confidence. They proposed that we quietly work our own little deposit until its proceeds enabled us to buy the adjoining fields. We have now been carrying out this plan for some time and installed a hydraulic press to assist us. As I said, that press has broken down, and we require your advice. We must, however, protect our secret carefully. If people learned that hydraulic engineers were visiting our little house, it would soon attract attention and cause people to ask questions. If the facts emerged, our chance of buying those fields and fulfilling our plans would disappear. That is why I insisted on your promising to tell nobody that you are going to Eyford tonight. I hope I have made everything clear?’

“‘I understand,’ I said. ‘There is only one point that I do not quite understand. How does a hydraulic press help you extract fuller’s-earth? As I understand it, the earth is dug from a pit like gravel.’

“‘Ah!’ he replied casually, ‘we have a special method. We press the earth into bricks, allowing us to transport it without revealing its nature. A mere detail, though. I have now confided everything, Mr. Hatherley, and demonstrated my trust in you.’ He stood. ‘Then I shall expect you at Eyford at 11:15.’
“‘I shall certainly meet you there.’
“‘And not a word to anyone.’ He gave me one last prolonged, searching look, gripped my hand in his cold, clammy one, and hurried out.

“When I considered everything calmly afterwards, you can imagine how astonished I was by the sudden commission entrusted to me. On the one hand, naturally I welcomed it. The payment was at least ten times the fee I would have named for my own services, and this work might lead to further commissions. On the other hand, my client’s face and manner had left a distinctly unpleasant impression. His explanation about the fuller’s-earth did not seem sufficient to justify either my coming at midnight or his extreme anxiety that nobody should learn of my errand. Nevertheless, I put all those fears aside, ate a hearty supper, and drove to Paddington. I set out having obeyed his demand for silence to the letter.

“At Reading I had to change stations as well as trains. Still, I caught the last train for Eyford and reached its small, dimly lit station after eleven. I alone got out. The platform was empty except for a sleepy porter carrying a lantern. As I passed out through the wicket gate, however, I found the man I had met that morning waiting on the other side in the shadows. Without speaking, he caught my arm and hurried me into a carriage with its door standing open. He raised both windows, tapped on the woodwork, and we set off as fast as the horse could manage.”
“Only one horse?” Holmes interrupted.
“Yes, just the one.”
“Did you notice its colour?”
“Yes. I saw it clearly by the carriage lamps as I climbed in. It was chestnut.”
“Did it look tired or fresh?”
“Fresh, certainly, with a glossy coat.”
“Thank you. Forgive the interruption. Please go on with this most interesting account.”

“We drove for at least an hour. Colonel Lysander Stark had said seven miles, but judging by our apparent speed and the time it took, I would put the distance nearer twelve. During the entire journey he sat beside me without saying a word. More than once I glanced towards him and found him watching me intently. The local roads must be poor, because the carriage jolted and lurched terribly. I tried to look outside and discover where we were, but frosted glass obscured the windows. I could make out nothing of the countryside except the occasional bright blur as we passed a light. Now and then I ventured a remark to break the journey’s monotony. The colonel answered in single syllables, and conversation soon died. At last the rough road gave way to the smooth crunch of a gravel drive, and we stopped. Colonel Stark jumped out and, as I followed, hurried me into a porch directly in front of us. We seemed to step straight from the carriage into the hall. I had not even a momentary glimpse of the house’s front. As soon as I crossed the threshold, the door slammed heavily shut. I faintly heard the carriage wheels rattling away.

“Inside the house, everything was utterly dark. The colonel fumbled about in search of matches, muttering to himself. Suddenly a door opened at the passage’s far end, throwing a long golden beam towards us. It widened, and a woman appeared, holding a lamp above her head and leaning forward to peer at us. She was pretty. The sheen of her dark dress in the lamplight told me its fabric was expensive. She spoke a few words in a foreign language, apparently asking a question. My companion answered with a single gruff word. She started so violently she almost dropped the lamp. Colonel Stark approached, whispered in her ear, and pushed her back into the room. After that he walked back towards me, now carrying the lamp in his own hand.

“‘Please wait here a few minutes,’ he said, opening another of the doors. The small, quiet room was simply furnished, with several German books scattered across a round table at its centre. Colonel Stark set down the lamp on a harmonium near the door. ‘I shall be back immediately,’ he said, and disappeared into the dark.

“I examined the books. Although I know no German, I could tell that two were scientific works and the others poetry. I went to the window, hoping to glimpse the surrounding countryside, but a barred oak shutter covered it. The house was extraordinarily quiet. Somewhere in the passage an old clock ticked loudly; otherwise everything was deathly still. A vague uneasiness began to trouble me. Who were these Germans, and why did they live in this strange, remote spot? Where was the place at all? I knew only that I was about ten miles from Eyford, with no idea whether north, south, east, or west. Reading, and perhaps other large towns, lay within that distance, so we might not be isolated after all. Yet the absolute silence convinced me we were in the country. I paced the room, humming softly to sustain my courage, and felt I was thoroughly earning my fifty guineas.

“Suddenly, without any warning sound in that profound stillness, the door slowly opened. The woman stood in the open doorway, the dark passage behind her and my lamp’s yellow light on her beautiful, intent face. I saw at once that she was sick with fear, and the sight chilled my own heart. Raising a trembling finger for silence, she directed a few hurried, whispered words of broken English towards me. Her eyes, like a frightened horse’s, kept darting back into the darkness.
“‘I would go,’ she said, apparently struggling to sound calm. ‘I would go away. I would not remain in this house. You can do no good.’
“‘But, madam, I have not done the work I came for. I cannot leave before I have examined the machine.’

“‘Waiting is not worth your while,’ she continued. ‘The door is open to you. Nobody stops you.’ When I smiled and shook my head, she suddenly cast aside all her restraint. She stepped forward, wringing her hands. ‘For Heaven’s sake!’ she whispered. ‘Leave before it is too late!’

“But I am naturally stubborn, and an obstacle only makes me more determined to see a thing through. I thought of my fifty guineas, the exhausting journey, and the unpleasant night ahead. Was all that to be wasted? Why creep away with the work undone and without the payment that was due to me? For all I knew, this woman might be suffering from some fixed delusion. Though her manner had shaken me more than I wished to admit, I put on a brave face, shook my head again, and declared I would stay. She was about to plead further when a door slammed upstairs and several footsteps sounded on the staircase. She listened briefly, lifted her hands in despair, and vanished as silently and suddenly as she had appeared.
“The arrivals were Colonel Stark and a short, stout man with a grey, chinchilla-coloured beard growing from the folds of a double chin. He was introduced as Mr. Ferguson.
“‘This is my secretary and manager,’ said the colonel. ‘Incidentally, I was under the impression that I left this door closed. I fear you must have felt a draught.’
“‘Quite the reverse,’ I replied. ‘I opened it myself because the room was rather stuffy.’
“He gave me another of his suspicious glances. ‘Then perhaps we should begin,’ he said. ‘Mr. Ferguson and I will show you the machine upstairs.’
“‘I suppose I should put on my hat.’
“‘No need. It is inside the house.’
“‘What? You dig out fuller’s-earth inside the house?’
“‘No, no. We only compress it here. But that is beside the point. We simply need you to examine the machine and tell us what has gone wrong.’

“We climbed the stairs, the colonel leading with the lamp and the stout manager following with me. The old house was a maze of corridors, passages, narrow spiral stairs, and small low doors with thresholds worn hollow by generations of feet. Upstairs there were no carpets or visible furnishings. The plaster was peeling away from the walls, where damp showed in sickly green patches. I tried to maintain an air of complete unconcern. Though I had ignored the woman’s warning, I had not forgotten it, and watched both men closely. Ferguson seemed surly and taciturn. From his few remarks, however, I could tell he was at least a fellow Englishman.
“Eventually Colonel Stark stopped at a low door and unlocked it. Beyond lay a little square chamber barely large enough for the three of us. Ferguson stayed outside while the colonel showed me in.

“‘We are actually standing inside the hydraulic press,’ he explained. ‘It would be most unpleasant if someone started it now. This chamber’s ceiling is the bottom of the piston, which descends onto the metal floor with a force of many tons. Outside are small lateral columns of water which receive, transmit, and multiply the force in the way you understand. The machinery starts and runs readily enough, but its action has become stiff and it has lost some power. Perhaps you would be good enough to inspect it and show us how to correct the fault?’

“I took the lamp from him and made a very thorough examination of the machinery. It was enormous, capable of tremendous pressure. Stepping outside, I lowered its control levers. The resulting swishing immediately told me that a small leak allowed water to flow back through one side cylinder. When I examined it more closely I found that an india-rubber band around the head of a driving rod had shrunk, leaving it too small to fill the socket in which it moved. That clearly explained the loss of power. I pointed it out, and the men listened carefully, asking several practical questions about the repair. Once I had made the explanation clear to them, I returned to the main chamber for another look, simply in order to satisfy my own curiosity about it. At a glance, the fuller’s-earth explanation was plainly false. Such a powerful engine would be absurdly excessive for that purpose. Wooden walls enclosed a floor formed by a great iron trough. Inspecting it, I noticed a crust of metallic deposits covering the surface. I bent down and began scraping some away to identify it. At that moment I heard a muttered German exclamation and looked up to see the colonel’s corpse-like face above me.
“‘What are you doing?’ he demanded.

“I was angry at having been deceived by the elaborate story he had told me. ‘I was admiring your fuller’s-earth,’ I replied. ‘I think I could give you better advice about this machine if I knew the exact purpose for which you use it.’
“The moment I said it, I regretted my recklessness. His face hardened, and a murderous light appeared in his grey eyes.

“‘Very well,’ he said. ‘You shall learn everything about it.’ He stepped back, slammed the little door, and locked it. I rushed towards the door and pulled hard at its handle, but the door held firm against every kick and shove. ‘Hello!’ I shouted. ‘Hello! Colonel! Let me out!’

“Then a sound broke the silence that made my heart leap in terror: the clank of the levers and the swish of the leaking cylinder. He had started the press. My lamp remained on the floor where I had set it to examine the trough. In its light I saw the black ceiling descending, slowly and unevenly. Nobody knew better than I that within a minute its force would crush me into an unrecognisable mass. Screaming, I hurled myself against the door and clawed at the lock. I begged the colonel to release me, but the relentless machinery drowned my cries. The ceiling was now only a foot or two above my head. Raising my hand, I could feel its hard, rough underside. Suddenly I realised that the pain of dying would depend largely on my position. Face down, I would receive the weight on my spine. I shuddered at the thought of that dreadful crack. Perhaps lying on my back would be easier—but could I bear to watch the deadly black shadow wavering down towards me? Already I could no longer stand upright. Then I saw something that sent hope flooding back.

“As I said, though the floor and ceiling were iron, the walls were wooden. One last desperate glance revealed a thin yellow line between two boards. It widened as a small panel slid back. For an instant I could scarcely believe this really was a doorway away from death. The next moment I flung myself through it and lay half fainting on the other side. The panel shut behind me. My lamp smashed, and a few seconds later the two iron surfaces clanged together, telling me how narrowly I had escaped.

“A frantic tug at my wrist brought me to myself. I lay on the stone floor of a narrow passage. A woman bent over me, pulling with her left hand and holding a candle in her right. It was the kind protector whose warning I had so foolishly dismissed.
“‘Come! Come!’ she gasped. ‘They will arrive in a moment. They will find you gone. Oh, do not waste precious time. Come!’

“This time, at least, I did not disregard her advice. I staggered to my feet and ran beside her down the corridor and a winding staircase. The stairs led into another broad passage. Just as we reached it, we heard running feet and two voices shouting to each other, one on our own floor and the other from below. My guide stopped and looked around, apparently at a loss for what to do. Then she threw open a door into a bedroom where bright moonlight streamed through the window.
“‘Your only chance,’ she said. ‘It is high, but perhaps you can make the jump.’

“As she spoke, a light appeared at the passage’s far end. Colonel Stark’s lean figure rushed towards us, a lantern in one hand and something like a butcher’s cleaver in the other. I ran across the bedroom, opened the window, and looked down. How peaceful, lovely, and wholesome the garden looked under the moon! The drop could be no more than thirty feet. I climbed onto the sill, but waited before jumping to hear what passed between my rescuer and the brute pursuing me. If he hurt her, I was determined to return and help, whatever the risk. Scarcely had I thought it when he reached the door and tried to push past her. She threw her arms around him, struggling to restrain him.
“‘Fritz! Fritz!’ she cried in English. ‘Remember what you promised after last time. You said it would never happen again. He will keep silent! Oh, he will!’

“‘You are mad, Elise!’ he shouted, trying to free himself. ‘You will destroy us. He knows too much. Stand aside!’ He flung her away, rushed to the window, and struck at me with the heavy blade. I had lowered myself and was hanging from the sill by my hands when the blow came. I felt a dull pain; my grip failed, and I dropped into the garden.

“The fall shook me but did not injure me. Knowing I was still far from safe, I picked myself up and ran through the bushes as fast as possible. Suddenly a terrible dizziness and nausea overcame me. I glanced down at my painfully throbbing hand and saw for the first time that my thumb was gone and blood was streaming from the wound. I tried to bind it with my handkerchief. Then a sudden buzzing filled my ears, and I collapsed unconscious among the rose bushes.

“I cannot say how long I lay unconscious, but it must have been many hours. The moon had already sunk out of sight and a bright morning was beginning when I woke. Dew soaked all my clothes, and blood from the thumb wound had drenched my coat sleeve. Its burning pain instantly brought back every detail of the night. I jumped up, afraid my pursuers might still be near. To my astonishment, however, neither house nor garden was visible. I had been lying in a corner of a hedge beside the main road. A little farther down stood a long building. As I approached, I recognised the very station at which I had arrived the previous night. Without that dreadful wound, everything I had endured might have been a nightmare.

“Still dazed, I entered the station and asked about a morning train. One would leave for Reading in less than an hour. The porter on duty was the same man who had been there when I arrived. Had he heard of Colonel Lysander Stark? He did not know the name. Had he noticed a carriage waiting for me the night before? No. Was there a police station nearby? Yes, about three miles away.

“I was too weak and ill to go so far. I decided to wait until I reached London before approaching the police. I arrived a little after six and went first to have the wound dressed. The doctor kindly brought me here afterwards. I now place the affair in your hands and will follow your advice exactly.”
For a while after this astonishing account, neither of us spoke. Then Holmes took from a shelf one of the heavy scrapbooks in which he stored newspaper cuttings.

“This advertisement will interest you,” he said. “It ran in all the papers about a year ago. Listen: ‘Missing since the ninth of this month: Mr. Jeremiah Hayling, twenty-six, hydraulic engineer. He left his lodgings at ten in the evening and has not been heard from since. He was wearing’—and so on. Ah! I suspect that was the previous occasion on which the colonel needed his machinery serviced.”
“Good heavens!” my patient cried. “Then that explains the woman’s words.”

“Certainly. The colonel is clearly cold-blooded and desperate, determined to let nothing interfere with his scheme. He is like those utterly ruthless pirates who leave nobody alive aboard a captured vessel. Every moment is precious to us now. If you feel able, let us go straight to Scotland Yard and arrange our journey to Eyford.”

About three hours later we were all aboard a train from Reading to the little Berkshire village: Holmes, the hydraulic engineer, Inspector Bradstreet of Scotland Yard, a plain-clothes officer, and I. Bradstreet spread an Ordnance map across the seat and used compasses to draw a circle centred on Eyford.
“There,” he said. “A circle with a ten-mile radius around the village. The house must be somewhere near its edge. You said ten miles, I believe, sir?”
“We drove for a good hour.”
“And you suppose they carried you that entire distance back while you were unconscious?”
“They must have. I also have a rather confused recollection of being lifted up and carried somewhere.”
“What puzzles me,” I said, “is why they spared you after finding you unconscious in the garden. Perhaps the woman’s pleas softened the villain.”
“I very much doubt it. I have never seen a more merciless face.”
“We shall soon discover all that,” Bradstreet replied. “Well, I have now drawn my circle on the map. I only wish I knew where along it to find the people we want.”
“I believe I could point to the spot,” Holmes said quietly.
“Really!” the inspector exclaimed. “You have formed an opinion already, then! Let us see who agrees. I choose south: the countryside is more deserted there.”
“I choose east,” my patient said.
“West for me,” the plain-clothes officer remarked. “There are several secluded little villages that way.”
“And I choose north,” I said. “There are no hills in that direction, and our friend noticed no climb during the drive.”
“Well!” the inspector laughed. “A fine range of opinions! Between us we have covered the compass. Who gets your deciding vote?”
“Every one of you is wrong.”
“But surely we cannot all be wrong.”
“Indeed you can. Here is my choice.” He touched the centre of the circle. “This is where we shall find them.”
“But the twelve-mile journey!” Hatherley gasped.
“Six miles out and six back. Perfectly simple. You said the horse was fresh and glossy when you entered the carriage. How could it look like that after twelve miles on bad roads?”
“A plausible trick, certainly,” Bradstreet said thoughtfully. “And of course we can have no doubt what sort of gang they are.”
“None,” Holmes replied. “They manufacture counterfeit coins on a large scale. They have used the machine to form the amalgam they substitute for silver.”

“We have known for some time that a very skilful gang was operating,” the inspector said. “They have produced half-crowns by the thousand. We tracked them as far as Reading, then lost the trail. They covered their movements like experienced hands. Thanks to this lucky accident, however, I believe we have finally caught them.”

The inspector was mistaken. These criminals were not destined to face justice. As we entered Eyford Station, we saw an enormous column of smoke rising behind a nearby cluster of trees. It hung over the countryside like a gigantic ostrich feather.
“Is a house burning?” Bradstreet asked as the train steamed away again on its journey.
“Yes, sir!” the station-master replied.
“When did the fire start?”
“During the night, I hear, sir. But it has spread, and now the whole place is ablaze.”
“Who owns the house?”
“Dr. Becher does.”
“Tell me,” the engineer interrupted, “is he a very thin German with a long, pointed nose?”

The station-master laughed heartily. “No, sir. Dr. Becher is English, and nobody in the parish fills his waistcoat better. But a foreign gentleman is staying with him, a patient, I understand. A little good Berkshire beef would do that one no harm.”

Before he had finished, we were all hurrying towards the blaze. The road climbed over the crest of a low hill. Ahead stood a large, sprawling, whitewashed house with flames pouring from every window and crevice. Three fire engines in the front garden struggled vainly to control them.
“That is the house!” Hatherley cried excitedly. “There is the gravel drive, and those are the rose bushes where I fell. I jumped from that second window.”

“At least you have taken your revenge on them,” Holmes said. “There can be no doubt that your oil lamp ignited the wooden walls when the press crushed it. They were probably too excited by the pursuit to notice the fire at the time. Now keep a careful watch on this crowd for your acquaintances of last night, though I very much fear they are a good hundred miles away already.”

His fears proved justified. From that day to this, nothing has been heard of the beautiful woman, the sinister German, or the surly Englishman. Early that morning a countryman saw a cart carrying several people and very large boxes travelling rapidly towards Reading. There the fugitives’ trail ended. Even Holmes’s ingenuity never uncovered the slightest clue to their whereabouts.

The firemen had been much disturbed by the strange arrangements they found inside the house, and still more by a freshly severed human thumb on a second-floor window sill. Around sunset their efforts finally succeeded and they managed to bring the flames under control. By then the roof had collapsed and the building was utterly ruined. Apart from twisted cylinders and iron pipes, nothing remained of the machinery that had cost our unfortunate acquaintance so dearly. An outbuilding contained large quantities of nickel and tin, but not a single coin could be found. That might explain the bulky boxes I have mentioned.

How the engineer reached the place where he regained consciousness might have remained a mystery, but the soft earth left us a very clear account of what had happened. He had evidently been carried to that spot by two people, one with remarkably small feet, the other with unusually large ones. Most likely the taciturn Englishman, either less daring or less murderous than his companion, had helped the woman take the unconscious man out of danger.
“Well,” our engineer said sadly as we sat down for the return to London, “what a fine affair for me! I have lost my thumb and a fifty-guinea fee. What have I gained?”
“Experience,” Holmes replied, laughing. “That may have an indirect value. Put it into words, and you can earn a reputation as excellent company for the rest of your life.”
